The 2027 total solar eclipse from a private dahabiya

The moon has fixed the date, the hour and the six minutes. This is how to be standing on a private dahabiya on the Nile at Luxor when they arrive.

{{FOUNDER_NAME}}  ·  October 2026  ·  13 minute read

By {{FOUNDER_NAME}}, Sillage Égypte journey designer · Egyptology reviewed by Dr. Azmy Salama, Egyptologist, Archaeologist & Private Guide · Last updated October 2026

The 2027 eclipse: the short answer

Quick answer. On Monday 2 August 2027 a total solar eclipse crosses Luxor. Totality lasts about six minutes and twenty-two seconds, from roughly 13:02 to 13:08 local time (Egypt summer time). It is the longest total eclipse visible from land since 1991, and none will be longer until 2114. It can be watched on a private tour: a dahabiya chartered whole for your party, with your own Egyptologist aboard. The date is under ten months away, so the best boats and rooms are the first to go. We have secured dahabiya and hotel availability for the date, and the choice narrows every month.

WhatTotal solar eclipse: the moon fully covers the sun
WhenMonday 2 August 2027
Totality at LuxorAbout 6 minutes 22 seconds, roughly 13:02 to 13:08 local time (Egypt summer time)
The longest totalityAbout 6 minutes 23 seconds, in Egypt south-east of Luxor; Luxor is within seconds of it
Partial phases at LuxorRoughly 11:40 to 14:30 local time, about two hours forty-five minutes in all
The pathSpain, Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, Libya, Egypt, then Saudi Arabia, Yemen and Somalia
The recordThe longest total eclipse visible from land since 1991; no longer one until 2114. The 2009 eclipse was longer, at sea.
Weather prospectsAugust in Luxor is near-cloudless, among the clearest skies on the path
The catchAverage daytime highs around 40 to 41 °C
Eye safetyCertified ISO 12312-2 eclipse glasses outside totality; naked eye only during totality itself
With SillagePrivate journeys built around the date, on the framework of The Complete Egypt, which starts from €7,500 per person (as of September 2026). The eclipse version is priced at 20% above our regular rate for the same journey, so from about €9,000 per person.

Every other decision in Egypt travel is negotiable: the dates, the route, the hotel. This one is not. The moon has fixed the date, the hour and the six minutes, and everything else on this page is about where you will be standing when they arrive. Sillage Égypte, the private Egypt journey designer, is building private journeys around that Monday. This post says what the eclipse is, why Luxor is one of the best places on Earth for it, what watching from a private dahabiya looks like, and when the boats and rooms will be gone.

The facts: date, time, duration

The total solar eclipse falls on Monday 2 August 2027. Over Luxor, totality (the moon passing fully in front of the sun) lasts about six minutes and twenty-two seconds, from around 13:02 to around 13:08 local time, with the partial phases bookending the late morning and early afternoon. The moon's shadow enters from the Atlantic, crosses southern Spain, then Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, Libya and Egypt, and leaves over Saudi Arabia, Yemen and Somalia into the Indian Ocean. Partial phases will be visible across nearly all of Europe, most of Africa, the Middle East and South Asia, but totality belongs to a corridor a few hundred kilometres wide, and Luxor sits close to the best of it.

Six minutes matters more than it sounds. Most totalities last two or three minutes. This is the longest total eclipse visible from land since 1991, and a longer one will not occur until 2114. (The July 2009 eclipse ran longer, but its longest minutes fell over the Pacific.) Add Luxor's August climatology, essentially cloudless and among the clearest on the path, and the geography makes its case without help. Our figures follow NASA's eclipse resources and published eclipse guides; see Sources at the end.

Why Luxor

The longest minutes and the clearest sky

The longest totality of the eclipse, about six minutes twenty-three seconds, falls in Egypt south-east of Luxor, and Luxor itself is within a second of it. The rival options are real but lesser: southern Spain is beautiful, coastal and nearer for Europe, with a much shorter totality and a genuine risk of sea cloud; Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia and Libya lie on the path with thinner tourism infrastructure; the Arabian stretches of the shadow cross remote country. Luxor combines near-maximum duration with very low climatological cloud and a city's worth of rooms, boats and four thousand years of surroundings. For duration and sky together, it is hard to name a better-arranged place.

A city built for the sun

There is also the matter of where this is happening. Karnak, the great temple of Amun-Ra, is widely described as laid out on a solar axis: its main axis is aligned on the winter-solstice sunrise, a point scholars still debate in its precision. Whatever the exact geometry, the priests who planned these temples were doing the astronomy this post is about. And early August, in the ancient calendar, fell in the season of the flood, the inundation that once rose over these fields before the dams tamed it. A total eclipse at high summer noon, over the city of Amun-Ra, on the river that made the year: our Egyptologists will be the first to say the astronomy needs no decoration, and the first to be unable to look away. Dr. Azmy Salama, our Egyptologist, will read the walls that morning; that is the difference between watching an eclipse and understanding where you watched it.

Watching from a dahabiya

A dahabiya, a shallow-draught traditional Nile sailing boat with a handful of cabins and a full crew, is chartered whole for one party. On eclipse day it is your private observatory: positioned with a clear horizon all round, the temples of the east bank behind you and the Theban cliffs to the west, crew at the rails with cold water, and no queue, rail or stranger's elbow between you and the shadow.

The day itself, hour by hour

  1. 05:15 — the last cool hour; cross to the west bank while the light is horizontal.
  2. 06:00 — the Valley of the Kings at first opening, three tombs in near-silence, finished before the heat builds.
  3. 08:30 — back aboard; breakfast as the boat settles at its mooring.
  4. 10:30 — the light hardens. Shutters, awnings, a long slow lunch on deck under shade.
  5. About 11:40 — first contact. The moon takes its first bite out of the sun, visible only through certified glasses. The deck goes quiet in a way boats rarely are.
  6. About 12:45 — the light turns metallic and thin, shadows sharpen eerily, the river turns pewter and the birds fly low.
  7. About 13:02 to 13:08 — totality. Your Egyptologist calls the last seconds of the partial phase, then glasses off: nothing between you and the corona. Twilight breaks around the whole horizon, the brightest planets and stars may appear, the temperature falls, and the river runs silver under a black sun.
  8. About 13:10 — your guide calls it, glasses back on for the departing partial; applause, of all things, from the crew.
  9. About 14:30 — the partial phase ends.
  10. 16:30 — tea on deck as the light softens; Luxor Temple, riverside and floodlit, after dark.

What totality feels like

Six minutes is long enough to do what shorter eclipses never allow: stop. The sky darkens to deep twilight in every direction at once, a sunset arranged around the whole horizon. The corona stands off the black moon in a way no photograph survives, the air cools by several degrees, and the birds settle as if persuaded it is evening. Veteran eclipse-chasers describe the first seconds as physical; our counsel is simpler. Put the camera down for at least three of the six minutes. You did not come this far to watch the moon's shadow through a viewfinder.

Why the river beats a roof or a coach park

Eclipse morning, the Corniche and every hotel roof in Luxor will be occupied, politely and densely, in the manner of every good viewing point on Earth. A boat of your own solves the geometry: your own horizon, your own shade, deck space per person instead of per hundred, and crew who answer to you. It also helps with the August problem, which is the honest one below.

The heat: honest counsel

August is the month we usually counsel travellers out of. Luxor's average daytime highs run 40 to 41 °C, hotter in spells, and the sun of early August stands high and unblinking from before seven until past six. The eclipse does not change the physics; it changes the arithmetic. For one week in the summer of 2027, one of the hottest places in Egypt is also one of the best on Earth, so the journey is built around the heat: monuments at dawn and dusk, the middle of the day aboard under awnings with the breeze off the water, hotels chosen for serious shade and serious air-conditioning, and a pace that treats noon as the enemy it is.

Heat is also a health matter, not just a comfort one. If anyone in your party is older, has a heart or blood-pressure condition, or does not cope well with high temperatures, speak to your doctor before booking. On board we plan for water, shade, rest and cooling, and we will tell you plainly if the week does not suit someone. If you can only bear Egypt in August once, this is the once. The rest of the year is compared, month by month, in when to go to Egypt.

Eye safety

Outside totality, wear certified eclipse glasses to the ISO 12312-2 standard for the whole partial phase, without exception. Sunglasses are not a substitute, and stacked sunglasses doubly not. During totality itself, and only then, the naked eye is safe, and it is the only way to see the corona properly. Every camera, phone lens and pair of binoculars needs a certified solar filter whenever any part of the sun is showing; an unfiltered telephoto can ruin a sensor in a second and an eye faster. The American Astronomical Society's eclipse safety guidance lists the standard and reputable suppliers. Sillage supplies certified ISO 12312-2 eclipse glasses to every traveller on the journey, so there is nothing to buy or bring.

The mistakes, all of them avoidable: watching through a phone screen and calling it protection; taking glasses off early because the sun "looks dim", when the thin crescent is precisely what burns; and the last-minute scramble for counterfeit glasses in a town full of visitors. On our boats your guide calls the start and end of totality, so nobody has to guess.

Availability and when to book: the private-tour question

Eclipse week will behave like festive week, compressed: a city's worth of worldwide demand arriving for a single Monday in what is normally the quietest month of the year. The good rooms, the suites and above all the small number of dahabiyas go first. The honest advice for a trip like this is to book twelve to twenty-four months out, and the date is now under ten months away, so we are already past the comfortable window. We have secured dahabiya and hotel availability for the date, but the choice of boats and suites narrows with every month. The maths is simple: Luxor has one Monday, the shadow has one width, and there are only so many boats on the river.

What an eclipse journey looks like

The framework is The Complete Egypt, a 13-day private journey that starts from €7,500 per person (as of September 2026), reshaped so the river sits under the shadow on the day: Cairo and the Grand Egyptian Museum first, the pyramids kept for a clean morning, then south so the boat is ready and the Egyptologist aboard well before 13:02 on the Monday. The eclipse version of the journey is priced at 20% above our regular rate, so from about €9,000 per person. Shorter shapes (Cairo, Luxor and the river) work for tighter diaries; the eclipse does not require a fortnight, though it earns one. Every version is private throughout: your own car, your own certified Egyptologist from first day to last, and a dahabiya chosen for your dates and chartered whole.
